paper.title: When Low Prediction Error Misleads Planning: Diagnosing Representation, Dynamics, and Decision Failures in Latent World Models
paper.abstract: Abstract The component that dominates a latent world model’s prediction error need not be the one whose repair most improves action selection. We show this by comparing action sequences from identical physical starts and separating endpoint error into a candidate-pool center and action-relative responses. Across four model families and four tasks, a confirmation pool of 256 new starts per task and 300 shared candidates per start shows that center error dominates MSE in 14/16 model–task cells. Yet in six of these cells, an oracle that corrects only the action-relative responses yields better physical rank correlation and top-30 elite quality than one that corrects only the center, while leaving more latent MSE (family-wise corrected intervals). The preference differs across the evaluated settings: a separate LeWorldModel (LeWM) study that executes oracle-selected actions favors center repair on PushT and on Reacher with a render-matched goal. Matched-candidate tests localize ordering loss: for LeWM, encoding realized endpoints raises physical Spearman from 0.464 to 0.975 on that Reacher setting and from 0.193 to 0.631 on PushT (64 starts per task), while Cube’s encoded-goal cost remains uninformative. A 72-run objective study improves selected response diagnostics, while incremental closed-loop planning gains remain unconfirmed. These results separate error magnitude from the decision effects of oracle correction and motivate evaluating representation, prediction, and planning as separate stages.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: World models encode observations, predict latent consequences of candidate actions, and optimize goal costs ( Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018 ; Hafner et al., 2019 ) , spanning joint-embedding predictive architectures ( LeCun, 2022 ; Assran et al., 2023 ; Bardes et al., 2024 ; Maes et al., 2026 , JEPA;) , latent-dynamics planners ( Sobal et al., 2025 ) , recurrent models ( Hafner et al., 2025 ) , and pretrained visual-feature predictors ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) . Low next-state error measures observed futures, not whether differences between alternative actions from the same state or planner cost orderings are correct ( Lambert et al., 2020 ) . Observational trajectories can couple state and action: recent motion can reveal the next action, while plausible actions share much of the successor state ( Shi et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) . Recent work targets this shortcut ( Gan et al., 2026 ; Chen, 2026 ) . A predictor may fit common evolution yet misstate counterfactual direction, scale, or ordering even while using its action input. Our framework fixes the physical start and varies future actions (Figure 1 ). Branch centering exactly partitions latent MSE into a center (common-mode) error shared by all candidate actions and an action-relative response error. Complementing training-time decompositions ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) and centered readouts ( Li et al., 2026b ) , we use this split to diagnose fixed checkpoints. The center term accounts for 62–89% of LeWM’s initial MSE at evaluated horizons; a controlled PushT intervention lowers long-horizon total MSE while increasing normalized response error, despite a frozen encoder. Decision utility adds a distinct test ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Chahe et al., 2026 ) . On 256 new starts per task, center error dominates MSE in 14/16 model–task cells across four additional families (80-comparison family-wise intervals). Yet in six cells, an oracle that replaces only the predicted responses with realized ones improves physical ranking and elite quality more than one that replaces only the center, while leaving more MSE (Table 1 ): the component that dominates the loss need not be the one that matters for decisions. An exploratory study on 64 starts per task compares predicted-outcome cost P P with encoded-realized oracle cost E E on identical candidates: E E improves both decision measures in 9/16 cells. Cube’s encoded cost remains uninformative across architectures. We then train six objectives across four tasks and three paired seeds (72 runs), evaluating rollouts up to H20 and, for three prespecified objectives, closed-loop success with each model’s native cross-entropy-method (CEM) planner on 1,024 paired source episodes. Some objectives improve response fidelity, most clearly on Reacher, while incremental cross-task CEM gains over a same-budget base remain unconfirmed. A direction-floor/amplitude-excess split distinguishes response shrinkage from direction recovery, revealing what a lower response loss actually changed (Figure 4 ). Our contributions are: 1. A matched-candidate test that locates where physical ordering is lost, and a confirmation on 256 new starts per task showing across four model families and four tasks that the error component dominating MSE need not be the one whose correction most improves physical decisions; Cube marks where the encoded-goal metric itself fails. 2. A same-start action-response fidelity protocol that exposes how aggregate latent MSE can improve while action-relative error worsens; exact center/response and scale–direction decompositions explain why inaccurate directions can reward response shrinkage under squared error. 3. A controlled 72-run objective study with closed-loop CEM evaluation showing that gains in selected response diagnostics can coexist with statistically unresolved incremental closed-loop gains.

sections.heading: 2 Related work
sections.text: Self-supervised learning established effective ways to avoid trivial representations, including BYOL’s bootstrapped targets ( Grill et al., 2020 ) and VICReg’s explicit variance–covariance regularization ( Bardes et al., 2022 ) . Decision-aware modeling instead asks which predictive information supports control, as formalized by value-aware losses ( Farahmand et al., 2017 ) and value equivalence ( Grimm et al., 2020 ) . PETS and Dreamer turn learned dynamics into action selection through trajectory sampling and imagined policy training, respectively ( Chua et al., 2018 ; Hafner et al., 2025 ) . These foundations motivate our question: which part of a latent prediction error matters for the decisions made from it? In latent world models, PhyLatent documents counterfactual local collapse despite LeWM’s global regularizer and reports training-time constraints with MPC gains ( Maes et al., 2026 ; Zeng et al., 2026 ) . ActSWM, CoCo and ATM target action-dependent prediction ( Gan et al., 2026 ; Shi et al., 2026 ; Chen, 2026 ) . DWM induces a world/action decomposition using an auxiliary world head and orthogonality constraint, while Dueling World Models centers action effects at readout ( Zhang et al., 2026b ; Li et al., 2026b ) . Our focus is post-training diagnosis: relating these action-relative errors to candidate decisions at fixed checkpoints. Counterfactual Quotient Models center successor measures; their implemented feature quotient is exact for feature-linear rewards ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . For point-latent predictors scored by squared goal distance, a common shift still enters candidate cost gaps. DA-LeWM measures latent–physical Spearman on sampled plans and CEM-stage candidates ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , while MCR directly trains candidate ordering ( Chahe et al., 2026 ) . Building on these decision measures, we pair predicted- and observed-outcome costs on identical realized candidates, then compare center-versus-response oracle repair with the MSE budget on new starts. Especially close, TRM audits an XY rowspace contributing little terminal latent MSE on shared TwoRoom candidates ( Li et al., 2026e ) . We instead repair components of prediction error and measure physical ranking and elite quality on the same candidates. The specific contribution is the measured mismatch between MSE dominance and oracle repair priority. Appendix A details connections to cost repair, output-rule changes, intervention analyses and recurrent-rollout controls.

sections.heading: Same-start branches.
sections.text: For each complete simulator state s s , we restore the identical state and execute K K alternative future action sequences. This yields paired physical trajectories, encoded outcomes z j z_{j} , and predictions p j p_{j} . Pairing by complete physical state removes variation in the initial observation, hidden velocity, and contact configuration. Multi-step branches after the first intervention are not described as pure one-step causal effects: their intermediate states legitimately differ because of earlier actions.

sections.heading: Physical criteria.
sections.text: Latent agreement is evaluated alongside normalized physical goal discrepancy: object position/angle for PushT, agent position for TwoRoom, joint coordinates for Reacher, and block position for Cube (Appendix C ). These endpoint scores are computed post hoc, not used as latent-goal costs or training targets; because the proxies differ, we do not pool them. In the four-candidate objective study, fixed-pool regret is the mean physical error among exact minimum-latent-cost ties minus the smallest physical error in that start’s candidate pool; it is not native CEM success.

sections.heading: Tasks and model families.
sections.text: We study PushT, TwoRoom, Reacher, and Cube. The primary model is LeWorldModel (LeWM), an end-to-end JEPA whose encoder is globally regularized toward an isotropic Gaussian and whose predictor is trained by next-latent regression ( Maes et al., 2026 ) . We also test final checkpoints of PLDM ( Sobal et al., 2025 ) , PreJEPA (a causal transformer on frozen DINOv2 patch features), DreamerV3 ( Hafner et al., 2025 ) , and DINO-WM ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) on all four tasks, without new training or checkpoint selection. Rendering, goal and posterior protocols are model specific (Appendix C ), so we compare architectures only through dimensionless within-model quantities.

sections.heading: Candidate pools.
sections.text: The C/S confirmation uses 256 new starts per task, shared across the four additional families and disjoint from the exploratory starts, with 300 candidates per start proposed by the final iteration of LeWM’s CEM; the comparisons therefore hold the proposer fixed rather than running each model’s own CEM (Section 7.1 ). The exploratory P/E study reuses 64 physical starts and realized endpoints per task across all five families, again with 300 LeWM-proposed action sequences per start. H5 response geometry uses fixed branch banks of 64 starts per task with K = 4 K=4 branches (Appendix C ).

sections.heading: Objective study.
sections.text: Each task’s pretrained LeWM encoder and projector are frozen and only latent prediction modules are updated. Six arms share initial weights, branch data, expert batches, optimizer, update budget and three paired seeds: a same-budget squared-error base , and objectives adding direction calibration, local branch geometry, true transition increments, an amplitude ablation, or a controlled combination. Each task uses 2,000 branch-training starts and 1,024 evaluation starts with four action candidates plus an independently sampled goal branch. Training uses H5; evaluation measures H1–H20, up to 100 environment steps, over 72 fine-tuning runs. Native CEM evaluates the initial checkpoint and base/transition/branch at three seeds on 256 paired source episodes per task: 10,240 model–episode evaluations but 1,024 distinct source episodes from the original training datasets.

sections.heading: Inference.
sections.text: Bootstrap resamples whole paired starts/source episodes rather than individual candidates or branches; fixed-checkpoint intervals condition on those models. The 64 reused starts support exploratory analyses; the fresh starts provide the separate confirmation test. Confirmation uses 100,000 paired-start draws and two-sided Bonferroni percentile intervals with nominal 95% family-wise coverage over 80 comparisons (Appendix F.2 ). Other comparison families and seeds are in Appendix C .

sections.heading: 7 Results
sections.text: The results form three layers that support different claims. Oracle replacements on fixed candidate pools (Sections 7.1 and 7.2 ) show which error component matters for physical action selection and where ordering is lost; the decomposition and response probes (Section 7.3 ) explain why error magnitude and decision effect can disagree; the objective and closed-loop studies (Section 7.4 ) test what learned corrections change. A historical positive control, in which removing LeWM’s global regularizer collapses the representation, lowers H5 prediction MSE by four orders of magnitude while closed-loop success falls on every task (Appendix J ); all results below concern healthy checkpoints.

sections.heading: 7.2 Matched candidates localize where physical ordering is lost
sections.text: For LeWM, across 64 starts and 300 identical candidates per task, the gap is graded rather than uniform: E E improves both ranking and elite quality on PushT and Reacher under eight-comparison family-wise intervals (Figure 2 ), ranking alone on TwoRoom, and neither on Cube, where both P P and E E correlations sit near zero. The P/E top-30 overlap ranges from 2.58 to 4.05 candidates, close to the random-overlap expectation of 3, so the two costs often choose nearly disjoint elites. A star marks a rank gain E − P E-P whose family-wise interval excludes zero (eight comparisons for LeWM; separate 32-comparison families for the feedforward and recurrent protocols). Exact values are in Appendix Table 7 . Figure 2 and Appendix Table 7 give the contrasts for all five model families. Across PLDM, PreJEPA, DreamerV3, and DINO-WM, E E beats P P on both criteria in 9/16 cells: all four PushT, three TwoRoom (PreJEPA/DreamerV3/DINO-WM), and two Reacher (PreJEPA/DreamerV3). Together with LeWM, these results distinguish two bottlenecks: ordering present in realized-outcome representations can be degraded by prediction, while Cube’s encoded-goal cost remains uninformative across all five families. Its same-pool selection gap persists even under E E ; the retrospective partition in Appendix C describes that gap without assigning a causal explanation. A descriptive control on the confirmation bank finds 155 Cube starts whose 300 physical scores are all distinct, and the four models’ mean E E correlations remain between − 0.062 -0.062 and 0.064 0.064 , so exact physical ties do not explain the Cube result (Appendix F.2 ). The conditioning controls clarify what P/E localizes. DreamerV3’s E E uses real intermediate observations and actions, so its gap includes recurrent state inference. Maximum available real history leaves all 12 feedforward P/E classifications unchanged but markedly improves PLDM/Reacher P P , identifying history availability as a contributor in that arm. Appendix C reports the control and its separate comparison family.

sections.heading: 7.3 Why the size of center error does not fix its decision effect
sections.text: Under squared goal cost, a center shift enters candidate cost gaps only through its projection onto candidate differences (Section 4 ), so the size of the center term does not fix its decision effect. Figure 3 reports the decomposition. At H5, the center term accounts for 68.0% of PushT, 76.7% of TwoRoom, 88.9% of Reacher, and 79.9% of Cube aggregate latent MSE; it remains 61.6–75.0% at H20. In the PushT direction-versus-base comparison at H20, the change in total state MSE is − 0.041 -0.041 [ − 0.050 -0.050 , − 0.032 -0.032 ] , while the change in Q Q is + 0.030 +0.030 [ 0.013 0.013 , 0.049 0.049 ] under a retrospectively specified 120-comparison family-wise correction (Appendix C ). A 0.046 0.046 reduction in center error masks a 0.0053 0.0053 increase in absolute centered-response MSE. This is the only one of the 40 task–contrast–horizon cells with opposite corrected movements in total MSE and Q Q , and it is a response-level mismatch: fixed-pool regret decreases in point estimate with an interval crossing zero, and no cell pairs a corrected MSE gain with a corrected regret loss. Section 7.1 tested the decision-level mismatch directly on matched candidates; Appendix D tracks center error and physical ordering along training. The action probes separate input sensitivity from response fidelity. Across all 20 final model–task checkpoints, mean-action masking or action permutation raises one-step prediction error on 512 fixed probe windows (Appendix Table 8 ); even the weakest, DreamerV3/PushT, worsens by 20%/34%. Unlike the 300-candidate CEM pools above, these K = 4 K=4 probes sample different actions; error shares are pool-dependent. On TwoRoom, PreJEPA and DINO-WM have near-unit gain (1.007 and 1.048) and higher predicted than true branch visibility, yet direction cosines of 0.432 and 0.288 and Q Q above the zero-response reference Q = 1 Q=1 . With full recurrent context, DreamerV3 on PushT has gain 1.003 but cosine 0.332; its Q Q grows from 0.837 at H1 to 1.339 at H5 as the cosine falls from 0.558 to 0.332, consistent with worsening direction agreement along the rollout. PLDM on TwoRoom supplies a healthy positive control ( Q = 0.067 Q=0.067 , cosine 0.967). Thus visible, correctly scaled branches can still point in the wrong latent direction: accurate action geometry requires direction as well as separation and gain.

sections.heading: 7.4 Objectives: response shrinkage and the closed-loop boundary
sections.text: Squared error can lower Q Q by shrinking responses rather than by correcting their direction. On PushT at H20, squared-error fine-tuning lowers the gain from 0.71 to 0.25: the base-minus-initial amplitude-excess contrast is − - 0.274 [ − - 0.332, − - 0.222] , whereas the direction-floor contrast of + + 0.007 [ − - 0.004, 0.019] spans zero. Other tasks do improve direction, and direction-plus-log-amplitude supervision improves PushT’s floor, although its fixed-pool regret interval spans zero (Appendix G ).

sections.heading: Preregistered response–decision comparison.
sections.text: A preregistered replication compares the squared-error and non-shrinkage objective classes on 2,048 fresh PushT starts, with four predictions fixed before these starts were collected. It reproduced the predicted H20 response ordering, with Q Q favoring squared-error objectives, but the fixed-pool regret difference was not resolved and the H5 Q Q prediction was contradicted; the sample size was set after the exploratory results but before the new data (Appendix H ). Changing the training objective thus altered response geometry without a confirmed change in fixed-pool decisions.

sections.heading: Closed-loop planning.
sections.text: Reacher transition improves offline H5 response error by 8.44% but changes CEM success by − 2.34 -2.34 points [ − 8.07 , 3.52 {-8.07},3.52 ] (Figure 4 e,f). All corrected transition-/branch-versus-base native-CEM success intervals cross zero. Separately, PushT base is − 6.64 -6.64 points below initial [ − 11.98 , − 1.43 {-11.98},{-1.43} ] (Appendix Table 6 ); that contrast measures the effect of shared fine-tuning rather than an added response loss. Recursive use of predictions adds a further source of sensitivity ( Talvitie, 2017 ) ; our equal-norm continuation probes and their negative controls (Appendices I.1 – I.3 ) reproduce the same signature with real-trajectory directions, so it is not specific to predictor error. sections.heading: 8 Limitations and conclusion
sections.text: The largest component of latent MSE can be the less valuable component to repair for action selection. Our new-start confirmation demonstrates this mismatch on identical candidate pools: response repair can improve physical ranking and elite quality more than center repair while leaving more prediction error. The scale–direction analysis explains why squared-error objectives can favor smaller responses even when their direction remains inaccurate. Together, these findings give world-model evaluation a concrete structure: test which physical distinctions the representation retains, which survive prediction, and which the planner converts into better choices. The preferred correction varies across the evaluated settings; the true-future oracles are diagnostic tools rather than deployable corrections. The confirmation extends start coverage within the studied tasks, while using a common proposer leaves generalization to other candidate distributions for future work. The objective-study and native-CEM evaluations draw on existing datasets, and possible pretraining overlap further limits claims about unseen trajectories. The objective studies make the next challenge concrete: learn response corrections from available observations and actions, without oracle access at decision time, and test their incremental benefit under matched-budget closed-loop planning.

sections.heading: Appendix A Extended related-work distinctions
sections.text: Our decomposition presupposes a representation worth predicting, continuing collapse-avoidance work in self-supervised learning ( Grill et al., 2020 ; Chen and He, 2021 ; Zbontar et al., 2021 ; Bardes et al., 2022 ) . LeWM regularizes embeddings toward a global isotropic Gaussian ( Maes et al., 2026 ) , while LpWM studies sparse, non-Gaussian codes ( Kuang et al., 2026 ) . More directly, PhyLatent documents physical and counterfactual local collapse despite LeWM’s global regularizer and reports training-time constraints with MPC gains on the same four task names ( Zeng et al., 2026 ) . We therefore take local non-collapse and branch separation as given and ask which component of a fixed checkpoint’s error matters for physical candidate decisions. A second line targets this counterfactual structure directly: ActSWM supervises predicted transitions to be separated and action-recoverable over long horizons ( Gan et al., 2026 ) ; CoCo imposes counterfactual consistency across inverse-action, zero-action, and mirrored rollouts to suppress visual-inertia shortcuts ( Shi et al., 2026 ) ; and ATM compares action information in encoded against predicted transitions ( Chen, 2026 ) . Branching web-agent data and predicted-state matching have also been used to distinguish alternative-action outcomes and improve action ranking ( Li et al., 2026c ) . Closer to our split, DWM adds an auxiliary world head with an action-invariance objective and couples it to the original prediction head through an orthogonality constraint, inducing complementary world and action components ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) . Dueling World Models subtracts each prediction’s mean action effect at readout; its gridworld control gain does not carry to its DMC CEM test ( Li et al., 2026b ) . Our use of the split is diagnostic rather than architectural: we decompose a fixed aggregate loss after training and test whether a controlled intervention lowers its common-mode term while raising its action-relative term (Section 4 ). Counterfactual Quotient Models center successor measures, preserving comparisons for bounded rewards in theory; their implemented feature quotient is exact for feature-linear rewards ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . We instead diagnose existing point-latent predictors scored by squared goal distance: a common latent shift is not an additive cost baseline, because it enters candidate cost gaps through a center–response cross term. A third line sidesteps fidelity and re-aligns the planning cost with decisions directly, as value-aware and value-equivalent models do ( Farahmand et al., 2017 ; Grimm et al., 2020 ) : DA-LeWM measures latent–physical rank correlation on sampled and CEM-stage candidates ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , Monotone Cost Ranking supervises candidate ordering for image-goal navigation ( Chahe et al., 2026 ) , TD-JEPA mines a temporal-progress cost from demonstration ordering ( Bai and Xiong, 2026 ) , and value-guided JEPA reshapes latent distance toward a goal-conditioned value ( Destrade et al., 2026 ) . TwoRoom cost repairs on frozen LeWM, including TRM’s shared-candidate audit of an XY rowspace contributing little terminal latent MSE , precede our prediction-error repair test ( Singh, 2026 ; Li et al., 2026e ) ; LEAP instead adds a learned terminal readout, action proposal and refinement to the released LeWM ( Pham and Bera, 2026 ) . ASAR changes the output rule instead: action-neighborhood reconstruction improves fixed-LeWM Cube execution, but its unretuned Reacher/PushT transfers are unresolved ( Li et al., 2026d ) . These gains show why our fixed-checkpoint oracle comparisons are not impossibility results for downstream planning. Our matched-candidate oracle (Section 5 ) diagnoses an existing predictor and native latent cost by testing whether the observed-outcome cost retains physical ordering that the open-loop cost loses on the same actions and outcomes. Decision-centric ladders separate prediction from utility ( Yu et al., 2026 ) ; Dual-Frontier proves passive non-identifiability of fixed-operator agent/world-model return attribution ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) . Our narrower test asks which latent error component an oracle should repair for physical ranking and elite choice on the same candidates, without return guarantees. The Intervention Gap already separates task-query capture from matched effect propagation in LeWM and PreJEPA ( Vakalis, 2026 ) ; our P/E and C/S tests instead compare physical rank and elite outcomes on the same candidates. Self-correction, Jacobian regularization, attenuation with information retention, and value-gradient weighting are established ( Talvitie, 2017 ; Fang et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Voelcker et al., 2022 ) . Recent work studies planner-reachable prediction error, latent transport, and recursive error in SG-JEPA ( You et al., 2026 ; Zhang and Jo, 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . Our equal-norm continuation probes (Appendix I ) build on this work with a narrower question about the direction of the error.

sections.heading: Action-use control.
sections.text: For each model–task pair we fix 512 probe windows (Table 3 ) and evaluate the final checkpoint only. The windows come from each model’s held-out validation split, except for DreamerV3, which was trained on all converted episodes without a held-out set. Masking replaces the action by the dataset-mean action, which is zero in the normalized action space of the JEPA-style models and the raw mean for DreamerV3, whose adapter consumes unnormalized actions; shuffling permutes whole action windows across the probe set with a fixed seed. PreJEPA and DINO-WM replace the action at all three context positions and score the pixel-embedding sub-block only, as in their training losses; DreamerV3 imagines one open-loop macro-step from the true posterior at each context position. Each cell of Table 8 is the loss increase divided by the true-action loss. The control is descriptive: one checkpoint per arm, no resampling interval, and magnitudes are not comparable across architectures because each loss lives in a different latent space. DreamerV3 contributes its single exported final checkpoint.

sections.heading: Appendix D Prediction error and candidate ranking along training
sections.text: We examine how prediction error and candidate ranking change across the ten saved epochs of each LeWM run. From epoch 1 to epoch 10, normalized prediction error falls by 82% on PushT, 68% on TwoRoom and 28% on Cube. Its center (common-mode) term falls by 88%, 75% and 32%, while response error Q Q falls by 22%, 30% and 1%, respectively. The exploratory pools (Appendix F.1 ) motivated the question; the new-start confirmation (Appendix F.2 ) supplies the reported intervals; and a LeWM first-replan study (Appendix F.3 ) executes the mean action of oracle-selected elites instead of scoring individual candidates.

sections.heading: Scope and estimator.
sections.text: This extends the completed P/E comparison to PLDM, PreJEPA, DINO-WM and DreamerV3 on four tasks. Each task has 64 start–goal pairs from 64 distinct evaluation episodes, reused across architectures: 256 pairs, not 1,024 independent physical starts. They are distinct evaluation episodes, which does not rule out overlap with pretraining data, and they form an existing exploratory sample rather than a new blind one. All models score the same 300 candidates from the final iteration of the LeWM CEM run and the same recorded physical outcomes, rather than each architecture’s own optimized proposal distribution or a new CEM execution. Feedforward predictions use the maximum available real causal history; DINO patch coordinates are not pooled. Dreamer E E is its recurrent posterior from recorded observations and actually executed actions, with the expert-path posterior goal, rather than a stateless endpoint image embedding. Candidates that terminate early are handled as in the LeWM P/E protocol (Appendix C ). For each start, with means p ¯ , z ¯ \bar{p},\bar{z} , modes are P j = p j , C j = p j − p ¯ + z ¯ , S j = z j − z ¯ + p ¯ , E j = z j . P_{j}=p_{j},\quad C_{j}=p_{j}-\bar{p}+\bar{z},\quad S_{j}=z_{j}-\bar{z}+\bar{p},\quad E_{j}=z_{j}. (10) C C preserves every pairwise predicted branch distance while correcting the center. S S retains the predicted center while correcting all centered responses. Their oracle information budgets differ: C C imports one true pool-mean vector, whereas S S imports the candidate-wise true centered responses. The S S – C C contrast therefore tests decision sensitivity to ideal component replacement, not which component is cheaper to learn or repair at equal information cost. Squared Euclidean cost uses every coordinate the model scores natively, computed in double precision. Spearman uses midranks, with constant ranks assigned zero; elites are the top 30 by stable candidate-index tie breaking. Elite physical error averages the selected candidates, not their action mean. The six paired contrasts per configuration are C − P C-P , S − P S-P and C − S C-S , each for correlation gain and elite-error reduction; positive favors the first mode. sections.heading: Why a large common error need not dominate selection.
sections.text: Writing p j = p ¯ + r ^ j p_{j}=\bar{p}+\hat{r}_{j} and goal z g z_{g} yields the elementary identity ‖ p i − z g ‖ 2 − ‖ p j − z g ‖ 2 = ‖ r ^ i ‖ 2 − ‖ r ^ j ‖ 2 + 2 ​ ⟨ p ¯ − z g , r ^ i − r ^ j ⟩ . \|p_{i}-z_{g}\|^{2}-\|p_{j}-z_{g}\|^{2}=\|\hat{r}_{i}\|^{2}-\|\hat{r}_{j}\|^{2}+2\langle\bar{p}-z_{g},\hat{r}_{i}-\hat{r}_{j}\rangle. (11) The shared scalar ‖ p ¯ − z g ‖ 2 \|\bar{p}-z_{g}\|^{2} cancels, but the center still affects ranking through its interaction with action differences. Center error is therefore not automatically harmless, and its squared magnitude alone does not measure its decision impact. The identity constrains how center error can act on selection; it does not describe how training produces either component. An exploratory, post-hoc recomputation on all 16 new-start confirmation cells measured this center projection on their saved 300-candidate pools. The six jointly supported inversion cells have normalized projection medians between .061 .061 and .414 .414 , overlapping the ten other cells. Thus near-orthogonality of center error to predicted candidate differences does not identify which cells favor S S ; the identity gives a geometric possibility rather than a cell-level mechanism. No inferential claim is attached to this diagnostic.

sections.heading: Numerical checks.
sections.text: Independent CPU audits recompute all costs in double precision and every bootstrap sample; using the original single-precision costs changes no status and no elite membership. A few starts have constant physical costs (two in PushT, one in Cube) and are retained. On average, 90.6% of Cube candidate pairs have distinct physical costs, and selecting the physically best 30 improves on random selection by .370, so these pools are not degenerate. Appendix F.2 tests the exploratory pattern on new starts.

sections.heading: Pre-specified scope.
sections.text: The exploratory result above selected the scientific question; it did not provide the following intervals. Before new forward evaluation, we froze 256 new physical starts per task, excluding the earlier exploratory starts, four fixed checkpoints (PLDM, PreJEPA, DINO-WM, DreamerV3), and the same 300 LeWM-proposed candidate sequences and physical outcomes at each start. The models have architecture-specific latent spaces and goals, so no latent MSE is compared across models. The physical starts are shared across models within a task, not 1,024 independent physical starts; pretraining-episode exclusion is not established. The same real-history and recurrent-posterior conventions as above are retained. This is a fixed-pool scorer comparison, not a new CEM search or execution of elite-mean actions. Besides P , C , S , E P,C,S,E defined above, write centered predicted and encoded candidate responses as R p = ( p j − p ¯ ) j R_{p}=(p_{j}-\bar{p})_{j} and R e = ( z j − z ¯ ) j R_{e}=(z_{j}-\bar{z})_{j} , with Frobenius norms A p , A e A_{p},A_{e} . The amplitude-only oracle (AMP) replaces R p R_{p} by ( A e / A p ) ​ R p (A_{e}/A_{p})R_{p} , keeping its normalized configuration. The structural oracle (SHAPE) replaces it by ( A p / A e ) ​ R e (A_{p}/A_{e})R_{e} , keeping predicted total response energy. Both keep the predicted center; if the response being rescaled has zero energy, the replacement is undefined and the prediction is left unchanged. SHAPE changes orientation, relative candidate lengths and branch-label configuration jointly. It has many more oracle degrees of freedom than AMP, so their comparison diagnoses which information matters rather than comparing equal-capacity trainable methods.

sections.heading: Restricted Flow-JEPA extension ( Huo et al., 2026 ) .
sections.text: Flow-JEPA generates a future segment jointly rather than one step at a time. On Reacher, we test two Flow-JEPA checkpoints with causal attention on 1,024 reused windows: at four intermediate steps the generated latent is replaced by P P , E E or one of four equal-norm residuals from other windows, and generation continues, averaging over sixteen paired flow-noise draws per window. The sixteen next-step and final-output contrasts form one family. All eight next-step intervals favor the residuals from other windows; seven of eight final-output contrasts do so and one is unresolved (at the fourth step the two outputs coincide). This tests continuation from substituted intermediate latents on one task, not Flow-JEPA’s native joint sampling or planning.

sections.heading: A fixed-reference continuation objective.
sections.text: We also asked whether training could exploit this sensitivity. Starting from three fixed 500-update base checkpoints per task, three objectives were each trained for another 500 updates (36 runs) with the same data, optimizer and update budget and with the encoder and projector frozen. The anchor objective combines one-step MSE on expert and branch data with 0.5 times the H5 rollout MSE. The joint objective adds 0.5 times the error of continuing each prediction p j p_{j} with the true preceding history, measured against the true next encoding e j + 1 e_{j+1} . The fixed-reference objective computes the same continuation error through a frozen copy of the initial network, so gradients reach the trained model only through its inputs; only the trained model is evaluated. Evaluation uses H20 rollouts on the same four 1,024-start banks. The four prespecified endpoints (H6 MSE, H20 MSE, H20 response Q Q , H20 physical regret), two contrasts (fixed-reference minus anchor and minus joint) and four tasks form a 32-comparison paired-start family. Against joint, nine endpoints worsen and seven are unresolved; against anchor, three improve, one worsens and twelve are unresolved; all eight regret contrasts are unresolved. A stale reference network and useful joint adaptation are candidate explanations that these endpoints do not separate.

sections.heading: Summary.
sections.text: These tests retain the condition-associated direction effect and the measured N / A N/A differences, while not supporting two stronger component explanations. They do not establish disjoint P/E domains, a full tangent space or why training creates the association, and the fixed-reference objective’s eight native-CEM comparisons remain unresolved. No secant result is attributed to Flow-JEPA. Independent CPU audits reconstruct all 56 reported contrasts.

sections.heading: Question and chronology.
sections.text: These follow-ups reuse the four 1,024-start, four-branch banks and sixteen fixed checkpoints of Appendix I.1 ; they are exploratory rather than an additional independent confirmation. Both families share each physical bank, and the three LeWM fine-tuning checkpoints share an encoder and are averaged before resampling. They ask whether the positive directional signature is specific to predictor error. In a locally linear reference with a constant map J J , permuting a marginally matched collection of normalized directions leaves average ‖ J ​ δ ‖ 2 / ‖ δ ‖ 2 \|J\delta\|^{2}/\|\delta\|^{2} unchanged. A positive L − X L-X gap therefore indicates an association with the conditional map beyond this constant-anisotropy case, not that the association is exclusive to errors produced by a predictor.

sections.text: Removing LeWM’s Gaussian regularizer supplies an extreme positive control (Figure 7 ). H5 raw latent prediction MSE falls to 1.8 × 10 − 6 1.8\times 10^{-6} – 2.5 × 10 − 6 2.5\times 10^{-6} across the four tasks, while closed-loop CEM success is 2%, 40%, 18%, and 48%, compared with 92%, 88%, 55.6%, and 74% for the corresponding healthy models. This historical comparison illustrates how target-space collapse can make latent prediction vacuous. Its heterogeneous evaluation sizes make it descriptive: most checkpoints use one 50-episode seed, while healthy Reacher uses a later five-seed re-evaluation. The main text concerns healthy checkpoints, whose prediction error is informative in aggregate but not about action selection. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC Zero arXiv:2610.05550v1 [cs.LG] 04 Oct 2026 When Low Prediction Error Misleads Planning: Diagnosing Representation, Dynamics, and Decision Failures in Latent World Models Rui Min Xianyao Li Fang Xu & Eric Jing Du Abstract The component that dominates a latent world model’s prediction error need not be the one whose repair most improves action selection. We show this by comparing action sequences from identical physical starts and separating endpoint error into a candidate-pool center and action-relative responses. Across four model families and four tasks, a confirmation pool of 256 new starts per task and 300 shared candidates per start shows that center error dominates MSE in 14/16 model–task cells. Yet in six of these cells, an oracle that corrects only the action-relative responses yields better physical rank correlation and top-30 elite quality than one that corrects only the center, while leaving more latent MSE (family-wise corrected intervals). The preference differs across the evaluated settings: a separate LeWorldModel (LeWM) study that executes oracle-selected actions favors center repair on PushT and on Reacher with a render-matched goal. Matched-candidate tests localize ordering loss: for LeWM, encoding realized endpoints raises physical Spearman from 0.464 to 0.975 on that Reacher setting and from 0.193 to 0.631 on PushT (64 starts per task), while Cube’s encoded-goal cost remains uninformative. A 72-run objective study improves selected response diagnostics, while incremental closed-loop planning gains remain unconfirmed. These results separate error magnitude from the decision effects of oracle correction and motivate evaluating representation, prediction, and planning as separate stages. † † footnotetext: 1 X. Min is with the Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL 32611, USA. † Corresponding author: Eric Jing Du, eric.du@essie.ufl.edu . First author: rmin@ufl.edu . Other author e-mails: xianyao.li@ufl.edu , xufang@ufl.edu . Figure 1: Overview of the diagnostic framework. (a) From one restored state, pair predicted and realized outcomes of alternative action sequences. (b) Separate center error from action-relative response error, then distinguish response scale from direction. (c) On identical candidates, compare predicted- versus realized-outcome costs ( P / E P/E ), and center- versus response-only oracle repairs ( C / S C/S ). (d) Test transfer from response fidelity to physical candidate ranking and elite quality, then closed-loop planning. Dashed arrows mark transfers assessed by separate tests. Latent geometry is schematic. 1 Introduction World models encode observations, predict latent consequences of candidate actions, and optimize goal costs ( Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018 ; Hafner et al., 2019 ) , spanning joint-embedding predictive architectures ( LeCun, 2022 ; Assran et al., 2023 ; Bardes et al., 2024 ; Maes et al., 2026 , JEPA;) , latent-dynamics planners ( Sobal et al., 2025 ) , recurrent models ( Hafner et al., 2025 ) , and pretrained visual-feature predictors ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) . Low next-state error measures observed futures, not whether differences between alternative actions from the same state or planner cost orderings are correct ( Lambert et al., 2020 ) . Observational trajectories can couple state and action: recent motion can reveal the next action, while plausible actions share much of the successor state ( Shi et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) . Recent work targets this shortcut ( Gan et al., 2026 ; Chen, 2026 ) . A predictor may fit common evolution yet misstate counterfactual direction, scale, or ordering even while using its action input. Our framework fixes the physical start and varies future actions (Figure 1 ). Branch centering exactly partitions latent MSE into a center (common-mode) error shared by all candidate actions and an action-relative response error. Complementing training-time decompositions ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) and centered readouts ( Li et al., 2026b ) , we use this split to diagnose fixed checkpoints. The center term accounts for 62–89% of LeWM’s initial MSE at evaluated horizons; a controlled PushT intervention lowers long-horizon total MSE while increasing normalized response error, despite a frozen encoder. Decision utility adds a distinct test ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Chahe et al., 2026 ) . On 256 new starts per task, center error dominates MSE in 14/16 model–task cells across four additional families (80-comparison family-wise intervals). Yet in six cells, an oracle that replaces only the predicted responses with realized ones improves physical ranking and elite quality more than one that replaces only the center, while leaving more MSE (Table 1 ): the component that dominates the loss need not be the one that matters for decisions. An exploratory study on 64 starts per task compares predicted-outcome cost P P with encoded-realized oracle cost E E on identical candidates: E E improves both decision measures in 9/16 cells. Cube’s encoded cost remains uninformative across architectures. We then train six objectives across four tasks and three paired seeds (72 runs), evaluating rollouts up to H20 and, for three prespecified objectives, closed-loop success with each model’s native cross-entropy-method (CEM) planner on 1,024 paired source episodes. Some objectives improve response fidelity, most clearly on Reacher, while incremental cross-task CEM gains over a same-budget base remain unconfirmed. A direction-floor/amplitude-excess split distinguishes response shrinkage from direction recovery, revealing what a lower response loss actually changed (Figure 4 ). Our contributions are: 1. A matched-candidate test that locates where physical ordering is lost, and a confirmation on 256 new starts per task showing across four model families and four tasks that the error component dominating MSE need not be the one whose correction most improves physical decisions; Cube marks where the encoded-goal metric itself fails. 2. A same-start action-response fidelity protocol that exposes how aggregate latent MSE can improve while action-relative error worsens; exact center/response and scale–direction decompositions explain why inaccurate directions can reward response shrinkage under squared error. 3. A controlled 72-run objective study with closed-loop CEM evaluation showing that gains in selected response diagnostics can coexist with statistically unresolved incremental closed-loop gains. 2 Related work Self-supervised learning established effective ways to avoid trivial representations, including BYOL’s bootstrapped targets ( Grill et al., 2020 ) and VICReg’s explicit variance–covariance regularization ( Bardes et al., 2022 ) . Decision-aware modeling instead asks which predictive information supports control, as formalized by value-aware losses ( Farahmand et al., 2017 ) and value equivalence ( Grimm et al., 2020 ) . PETS and Dreamer turn learned dynamics into action selection through trajectory sampling and imagined policy training, respectively ( Chua et al., 2018 ; Hafner et al., 2025 ) . These foundations motivate our question: which part of a latent prediction error matters for the decisions made from it? In latent world models, PhyLatent documents counterfactual local collapse despite LeWM’s global regularizer and reports training-time constraints with MPC gains ( Maes et al., 2026 ; Zeng et al., 2026 ) . ActSWM, CoCo and ATM target action-dependent prediction ( Gan et al., 2026 ; Shi et al., 2026 ; Chen, 2026 ) . DWM induces a world/action decomposition using an auxiliary world head and orthogonality constraint, while Dueling World Models centers action effects at readout ( Zhang et al., 2026b ; Li et al., 2026b ) . Our focus is post-training diagnosis: relating these action-relative errors to candidate decisions at fixed checkpoints. Counterfactual Quotient Models center successor measures; their implemented feature quotient is exact for feature-linear rewards ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . For point-latent predictors scored by squared goal distance, a common shift still enters candidate cost gaps. DA-LeWM measures latent–physical Spearman on sampled plans and CEM-stage candidates ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , while MCR directly trains candidate ordering ( Chahe et al., 2026 ) . Building on these decision measures, we pair predicted- and observed-outcome costs on identical realized candidates, then compare center-versus-response oracle repair with the MSE budget on new starts. Especially close, TRM audits an XY rowspace contributing little terminal latent MSE on shared TwoRoom candidates ( Li et al., 2026e ) . We instead repair components of prediction error and measure physical ranking and elite quality on the same candidates. The specific contribution is the measured mismatch between MSE dominance and oracle repair priority. Appendix A details connections to cost repair, output-rule changes, intervention analyses and recurrent-rollout controls. 3 Problem setup Let o t o_{t} be an observation, a t : t + H − 1 a_{t:t+H-1} an action sequence, ϕ \phi an observation-conditioned representation map (encoder or recurrent posterior), and f f a latent predictor; the horizon H H counts model steps of five environment steps each, and H5 denotes H = 5 H=5 . Starting from a shared context z 0 z_{0} , the model produces z ^ H = f ( H ) ( z 0 , a t : t + H − 1 ) , z H = ϕ ( o ≤ t + H , a < t + H ) . \hat{z}_{H}=f^{(H)}(z_{0},a_{t:t+H-1}),\qquad z_{H}=\phi(o_{\leq t+H},a_{<t+H}). (1) Standard latent prediction minimizes ‖ z ^ H − z H ‖ 2 \|\hat{z}_{H}-z_{H}\|^{2} , usually averaged over observational trajectories. A planner instead samples candidate sequences a ( j ) a^{(j)} , evaluates a latent goal cost d ⁡ ( z ^ H ( j ) , z g ) d(\hat{z}_{H}^{(j)},z_{g}) , and selects low-cost candidates ( Chua et al., 2018 ) . Prediction rewards pointwise agreement on observed futures; planning requires correct relative consequences across counterfactual candidates. Same-start branches. For each complete simulator state s s , we restore the identical state and execute K K alternative future action sequences. This yields paired physical trajectories, encoded outcomes z j z_{j} , and predictions p j p_{j} . Pairing by complete physical state removes variation in the initial observation, hidden velocity, and contact configuration. Multi-step branches after the first intervention are not described as pure one-step causal effects: their intermediate states legitimately differ because of earlier actions. Physical criteria. Latent agreement is evaluated alongside normalized physical goal discrepancy: object position/angle for PushT, agent position for TwoRoom, joint coordinates for Reacher, and block position for Cube (Appendix C ). These endpoint scores are computed post hoc, not used as latent-goal costs or training targets; because the proxies differ, we do not pool them. In the four-candidate objective study, fixed-pool regret is the mean physical error among exact minimum-latent-cost ties minus the smallest physical error in that start’s candidate pool; it is not native CEM success. 4 Why aggregate prediction error can mislead 4.1 Exact center/response decomposition For one starting state, define branch centers and centered responses z ¯ = K − 1 ​ ∑ j z j , p ¯ = K − 1 ​ ∑ j p j , r j = z j − z ¯ , r ^ j = p j − p ¯ . \bar{z}=K^{-1}\textstyle\sum_{j}z_{j},\quad\bar{p}=K^{-1}\sum_{j}p_{j},\qquad r_{j}=z_{j}-\bar{z},\quad\hat{r}_{j}=p_{j}-\bar{p}. The center denotes the sampled action-pool mean rather than physical null-action dynamics. The decision effect of center error thus depends on its projection onto candidate differences, rather than its norm alone. An exploratory projection check did not distinguish the six inversion cells of Section 7.1 from other cells (Appendix F.1 ); the identity explains how a reversal is possible under this score, while its empirical drivers remain to be established. 4.2 Response scale and direction Stack centered true and predicted responses into R R and R ^ \hat{R} . Inaccurate direction can thus reward shrinking the response, a response-level analogue of blurry squared-error video prediction ( Mathieu et al., 2016 ) ; forcing g = 1 g=1 can instead expand the wrong response. Interpreting the former as a monotone direction floor requires c ≥ 0 c\geq 0 : for c < 0 c<0 , the nonnegative-scale minimum is Q = 1 Q=1 at g = 0 g=0 , not 1 − c 2 1-c^{2} . Section 7.4 tests amplitude movement toward the least-squares scale rather than equating branch distance with fidelity. 5 Matched-candidate localization For each start, hold action sequences and physical endpoints fixed; d d is the model-native squared Euclidean latent goal score: P j = d ⁡ ( p j , z g ) , E j = d ⁡ ( z j , z g ) , q j = physical endpoint error . P_{j}=d(p_{j},z_{g}),\qquad E_{j}=d(z_{j},z_{g}),\qquad q_{j}=\text{physical endpoint error}. (6) Here z j z_{j} uses candidate j j ’s realized observations: an encoded endpoint for feedforward models and a real-observation recurrent posterior for DreamerV3. We report Spearman with q j q_{j} , the physical error averaged over selected top- k k candidates, and P/E elite overlap; executing the mean action is a separate operator. The four endpoint sets form a center/response 2 × 2 2\times 2 grid: P = ( p ¯ , r ^ ) P=(\bar{p},\hat{r}) , C = ( z ¯ , r ^ ) C=(\bar{z},\hat{r}) , S = ( p ¯ , r ) S=(\bar{p},r) , E = ( z ¯ , r ) E=(\bar{z},r) . Weak physical ordering under E E points to a bottleneck in the tested representation/goal metric. Stronger ordering under E E than P P places the loss between prediction and realized-state inference, which includes observation-conditioned posterior updates in recurrent models. Native CEM then tests how these candidate-level differences carry through search and replanning. 6 Experimental design Tasks and model families. We study PushT, TwoRoom, Reacher, and Cube. The primary model is LeWorldModel (LeWM), an end-to-end JEPA whose encoder is globally regularized toward an isotropic Gaussian and whose predictor is trained by next-latent regression ( Maes et al., 2026 ) . We also test final checkpoints of PLDM ( Sobal et al., 2025 ) , PreJEPA (a causal transformer on frozen DINOv2 patch features), DreamerV3 ( Hafner et al., 2025 ) , and DINO-WM ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) on all four tasks, without new training or checkpoint selection. Rendering, goal and posterior protocols are model specific (Appendix C ), so we compare architectures only through dimensionless within-model quantities. Candidate pools. The C/S confirmation uses 256 new starts per task, shared across the four additional families and disjoint from the exploratory starts, with 300 candidates per start proposed by the final iteration of LeWM’s CEM; the comparisons therefore hold the proposer fixed rather than running each model’s own CEM (Section 7.1 ). The exploratory P/E study reuses 64 physical starts and realized endpoints per task across all five families, again with 300 LeWM-proposed action sequences per start. H5 response geometry uses fixed branch banks of 64 starts per task with K = 4 K=4 branches (Appendix C ). Objective study. Each task’s pretrained LeWM encoder and projector are frozen and only latent prediction modules are updated. Six arms share initial weights, branch data, expert batches, optimizer, update budget and three paired seeds: a same-budget squared-error base , and objectives adding direction calibration, local branch geometry, true transition increments, an amplitude ablation, or a controlled combination. Each task uses 2,000 branch-training starts and 1,024 evaluation starts with four action candidates plus an independently sampled goal branch. Training uses H5; evaluation measures H1–H20, up to 100 environment steps, over 72 fine-tuning runs. Native CEM evaluates the initial checkpoint and base/transition/branch at three seeds on 256 paired source episodes per task: 10,240 model–episode evaluations but 1,024 distinct source episodes from the original training datasets. Inference. Bootstrap resamples whole paired starts/source episodes rather than individual candidates or branches; fixed-checkpoint intervals condition on those models. The 64 reused starts support exploratory analyses; the fresh starts provide the separate confirmation test. Confirmation uses 100,000 paired-start draws and two-sided Bonferroni percentile intervals with nominal 95% family-wise coverage over 80 comparisons (Appendix F.2 ). Other comparison families and seeds are in Appendix C . 7 Results The results form three layers that support different claims. Oracle replacements on fixed candidate pools (Sections 7.1 and 7.2 ) show which error component matters for physical action selection and where ordering is lost; the decomposition and response probes (Section 7.3 ) explain why error magnitude and decision effect can disagree; the objective and closed-loop studies (Section 7.4 ) test what learned corrections change. A historical positive control, in which removing LeWM’s global regularizer collapses the representation, lowers H5 prediction MSE by four orders of magnitude while closed-loop success falls on every task (Appendix J ); all results below concern healthy checkpoints. 7.1 MSE dominance does not determine oracle decision sensitivity On 256 new starts per task, 80-comparison family-wise intervals show MSE S > MSE C \mathrm{MSE}_{S}>\mathrm{MSE}_{C} in 14/16 cells. One cell has the opposite MSE ordering, and one interval spans zero. Six of the 14 favor S S on both physical criteria despite more MSE (Table 1 ); these cells lie in PreJEPA, DINO-WM and DreamerV3, across PushT, TwoRoom and Reacher. The earlier 64-start sample shows the same qualitative pattern (Appendix F.1 ). A separate LeWM study that executes the mean action of oracle-selected elites instead favors C C on PushT and render-matched Reacher (Appendix F.3 ), so the preferred correction differs across the evaluated settings. Those two tasks already favor C C in fixed-elite point estimates, so executing the elite mean did not create the preference; the two studies differ in models, pools and evaluation operator, and do not isolate which difference matters. The added result is the coexistence of better physical decisions and more residual MSE. These oracles are non-deployable diagnostics with unequal true-future information: SHAPE receives the true response vectors, whereas AMP receives their energy. Every CEM interval includes zero; task scores are not pooled. 8 Limitations and conclusion The largest component of latent MSE can be the less valuable component to repair for action selection. Our new-start confirmation demonstrates this mismatch on identical candidate pools: response repair can improve physical ranking and elite quality more than center repair while leaving more prediction error. The scale–direction analysis explains why squared-error objectives can favor smaller responses even when their direction remains inaccurate. Together, these findings give world-model evaluation a concrete structure: test which physical distinctions the representation retains, which survive prediction, and which the planner converts into better choices. The preferred correction varies across the evaluated settings; the true-future oracles are diagnostic tools rather than deployable corrections. The confirmation extends start coverage within the studied tasks, while using a common proposer leaves generalization to other candidate distributions for future work. The objective-study and native-CEM evaluations draw on existing datasets, and possible pretraining overlap further limits claims about unseen trajectories. The objective studies make the next challenge concrete: learn response corrections from available observations and actions, without oracle access at decision time, and test their incremental benefit under matched-budget closed-loop planning.
